'''Günter Harder''' (14 March 1938 – 10 June 2025) was a German mathematician, specializing in [[arithmetic geometry]] and [[number theory]].

==Education==
Harder studied mathematics and physics in [[University of Hamburg|Hamburg]] and [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]]. Simultaneously with the ''[[Staatsexamen]]'' in 1964 in Hamburg, he received his doctoral degree (Dr. rer. nat.) under [[Ernst Witt]] with a thesis ''Über die Galoiskohomologie der Tori''.<ref name="MG">{{MathGenealogy|id=21244}}</ref> Two years later, he completed his [[habilitation]].

==Career==
After a one-year postdoctorate position at [[Princeton University]] and a position as an assistant professor at the [[University of Heidelberg]], he became a professor ordinarius at the [[University of Bonn]]. With the exception of a six-year stay at the former [[Bergische Universität Wuppertal|Universität-Gesamthochschule Wuppertal]], Harder remained at the University of Bonn until his retirement in 2003. From 1995 to 2006, he was one of the directors of the [[Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik]] in Bonn.

He was a visiting professor at [[Harvard University]], [[Yale University]], at Princeton's [[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute for Advanced Study (IAS)]] (for the academic years 1966–1967, 1972–1973, 1986–1987, autumn of 1983, autumn of 2006),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/g%C3%BCnter-harder|title=Günter Harder – Scholars &#124; Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019|website=www.ias.edu|accessdate=16 December 2021}}</ref> at the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]] (I.H.É.S.) in Paris, at the [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]] in Mumbai, and at the [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute]] (MSRI) at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

For decades, Harder was known to German mathematicians as the ''Spiritus Rector'' for  a mathematical workshop held for one week in spring and one week in autumn; the workshop, sponsored by the [[Mathematical Research Institute of Oberwolfach]], introduced young mathematicians and scientists to important new developments in pure mathematics and mathematical sciences.{{cn|date=May 2024}}

Harder's doctoral students include [[Kai Behrend]], [[Jörg Bewersdorff]], [[Joachim Schwermer]], and [[Maria Heep-Altiner]].<ref name="MG"/>

==Death==
Harder died on 10 June 2025, at the age of 87.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn Mourns Death of Günter Harder {{!}} Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik |url=https://www.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/de/node/14490 |access-date=12 June 2025 |website=www.mpim-bonn.mpg.de}}</ref>

==Research==
His research deals with arithmetic geometry, [[automorphic form]]s, [[Shimura variety|Shimura varieties]], [[Motive (algebraic geometry)|motives]], and [[algebraic number theory]]. He made foundational contributions to the [[Waldspurger formula]].

With [[Ina Kersten]], he was a co-editor of the collected works of [[Ernst Witt]].

==Awards and honours==
Harder was an [[List of International Congresses of Mathematicians Plenary and Invited Speakers|invited speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1970 and gave a talk titled ''Semisimple group schemes over curves and automorphic functions''<ref>Harder, Günter, [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1970.2/Main/icm1970.2.0307.0312.ocr.pdf "Semisimple group schemes over curves and automorphic functions."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202001301/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1970.2/Main/icm1970.2.0307.0312.ocr.pdf |date=2 February 2017}} Actes, Congrès intern. Math. Tome 2 (1970): 307–312.</ref> and in 1990 with a talk titled ''Eisenstein cohomology of arithmetic groups and its applications to number theory''.<ref>Harder, Günter. [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1990.2/Main/icm1990.2.0779.0790.ocr.pdf "Eisenstein cohomology of arithmetic groups and its applications to number theory."] In Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, vol. 1, pp. 779–790. 1990.</ref> In 1988, he was awarded the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize|Leibniz Prize]] by the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft]].

In 2004, Harder received, with [[Friedhelm Waldhausen]], the [[von Staudt Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/node/101|title=Günter Harder &#124; Max Planck Institute for Mathematics|website=www.mpim-bonn.mpg.de|accessdate=16 December 2021}}</ref>
